code.title: Class vs struct: copy semantics and defaults

followUps:
The struct is boxed: a copy of it is allocated on the heap inside a new object, and the interface variable points to that box. Changes made through the interface change the box, not your original variable.

Example: IInc i = s; i.Inc(); raises the boxed copy to 1 while s.N stays 0. Each cast allocates again, so interface calls on structs in hot loops add GC pressure. Generic constraints (where T : struct, IInc) avoid boxing.

No. A struct is stored wherever its owner lives: in a local it is on the stack (or a register), but as a field of a class it is inside that heap object, in an array it is inside the heap array, and boxed it is on the heap.

Example: new Point[1000] is one heap block holding 1000 inline points. Locals can also be captured by lambdas, which moves them into a heap closure. So think "copied by value", not "on the stack".

code.title: Mutable struct bug: the list indexer returns a copy

followUps:
Because an array indexer does not return a copy: arr[0] is a direct reference to the element's memory (a variable), so the call mutates the real element.

A List<T> indexer is a method (get_Item) that returns the struct by value, so you edit a temporary copy. Example: with Counter starting at 0, the array shows 1 after one Increment() and the list still shows 0. Fix the list case by reading to a local, changing it, and writing it back (list[0] = tmp), or use CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan(list)[0].

It is a hidden copy the compiler makes of a struct before calling a member on it, so that a possibly-mutating member cannot change a read-only location.

It happens for readonly fields, in parameters and ref readonly locals when the struct is not readonly. Example: _t.Bump() on a readonly Tally _t bumps a copy, so _t never changes, and with a 64-byte struct you also pay 64 bytes of copying each call. Marking the struct readonly removes the copy.

code.title: Primary constructor parameters captured into hidden state

followUps:
Validate at the top of the class body or in a field initialiser, then store the checked value, because the parameter itself has no built-in validation.

class Svc(IRepo repo)
{
    private readonly IRepo _repo =
        repo ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(repo));
}

Using the field afterwards means the unchecked parameter is never captured. For records, validate in a property with an explicit initialiser, or in a constructor body.

Because a captured parameter is a hidden, mutable field with no name, no access modifier and no readonly, so state can change in surprising ways and reviewers cannot see it.

Example: a method does limit++ on the parameter, and another method reads the same name, so a hidden counter is now shared. It also differs from a field copy: if a property was initialised from limit too, you have two copies that drift apart (CS9124). Teams often require copying parameters into readonly fields explicitly.

code.title: Property vs public field: validation and computed members

followUps:
When a method is the better description of what happens: when it is slow or does I/O, can throw or fail, has side effects, returns a different value each call, or needs parameters.

A property should look like a field: cheap, repeatable and without surprises. Example: order.Total computed from 3 lines is fine, but GetCustomerFromDatabase() or ToList() (it allocates a new list each call) should be methods. Debuggers also evaluate properties automatically, which makes costly ones painful.

An init accessor compiles to a normal setter whose return type carries a required modifier, modreq(IsExternalInit), so only compilers that understand it allow the assignment at creation time.

At run time it is just a set_X method, which is why reflection can still call it (and older compilers can call it and ignore the marker). The immutability is a compile-time rule, not a runtime guarantee.

code.title: Get-only vs private set (init needs C# 9)

followUps:
Yes. At run time an init property is an ordinary setter, so PropertyInfo.SetValue works after construction; the read-only rule exists only in the compiler.

That is how serializers and ORMs fill init-only properties. A get-only auto-property is different: it has a readonly backing field, which reflection can also change, but that is a hack. Treat it as a bug if your own code does it, because other code may assume the value never changes.

with first clones the object, then runs the init accessors of the listed members on the clone, which is allowed because the clone counts as still under construction.

var p2 = p1 with { Age = 40 };
// = clone p1, then p2.Age = 40 (init)

This is why records can have init-only properties and still be changed "non-destructively": p1 is untouched and p2 is a new object with one different value.

code.title: Hand-written value equality, what a record generates

followUps:
Two records are equal only if they have exactly the same run-time type and equal members, because the generated equality checks EqualityContract.

Example: record Person(string Name) and record Student(string Name) : Person(Name). new Person("A") == new Student("A") is false even with the same name, which keeps equality symmetric. Derived records add their own members to the comparison. Equality through a base-typed variable still works correctly because Equals is virtual.

Write your own Equals and GetHashCode in the record and compare the list with SequenceEqual; the generated version compares the list reference only.

public virtual bool Equals(Order? o) =>
    o != null && Id == o.Id && Items.SequenceEqual(o.Items);
public override int GetHashCode() =>
    HashCode.Combine(Id, Items.Count);

Or store an immutable collection type with value semantics. The hash must use only fields that equal objects share.

code.title: Broken GetHashCode: HashSet misses an equal key

followUps:
Because string.GetHashCode() uses a random seed that changes each process start, so attackers cannot craft many strings with the same hash to slow a hash table to O(n) per lookup (a hash-flooding denial of service).

Example: "abc" may hash to 123 in one run and 987 in the next. So never store hash codes in files or databases, or compare them across processes; use a stable hash (such as SHA-256) for that.

It is the standard comparer the collections use when you do not give one: it calls IEquatable<T>.Equals if the type implements it, otherwise object.Equals.

Example: new HashSet<Point>() uses EqualityComparer<Point>.Default. For structs implementing IEquatable<T> this avoids boxing, which is why implementing it is a good habit. You can pass a custom comparer, for example StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase, to change the rule.

code.title: == vs Equals vs ReferenceEquals

followUps:
Overload == only on a class that is clearly a value object with immutable data, and then do it together with !=, Equals, GetHashCode and IEquatable<T>.

Doing it for an entity class is risky: callers expect == on classes to mean "same object", and a half-done overload gives surprises (null checks calling your operator, infinite recursion if you write this == null). Prefer a record, which generates everything consistently.

x is null is a pattern that always tests for a null reference and never calls an overloaded ==.

It compiles to a simple null check (ldnull; ceq). Example: if a class overloads == so that a == null returns true for an "empty" object, a is null still returns false. This makes is null the safest null test in generic or library code.

code.title: Defensive copy on a readonly field of a mutable struct

followUps:
You would use a tool that shows the generated IL or use analyzers, because defensive copies are invisible in the source.

Steps: turn on the analyzer for non-readonly struct members used in in or readonly contexts (IDE0250, IDE0251 suggest readonly), or open the code in ILSpy and look for extra local copies (ldobj, stloc) before the call. A benchmark that gets faster after adding readonly to a struct of 32+ bytes also confirms it.

A readonly ref struct is a stack-only type (ref struct) whose fields are all read-only, like ReadOnlySpan<T>.

It cannot be boxed, stored in a class field, captured by a lambda, or used across await, so it can safely point at stack memory or slices of arrays. The readonly part means no defensive copies when it is passed by in. Example: ReadOnlySpan<char> s = text.AsSpan(0, 3); slices without allocating.

code.title: Lazy singleton versus an injectable clock

followUps:
The CLR guarantees that a static field initialiser (or static constructor) runs exactly once, with a lock, before the first use, so a static readonly field is thread-safe to initialise.

static readonly Config Instance = new Config();
// or lazily:
static readonly Lazy<Config> L =
    new Lazy<Config>(() => new Config());

Only the initialisation is thread-safe; changing the object's fields afterwards still needs your own locking.

beforefieldinit is a flag on a type that has no explicit static constructor, which lets the runtime run the static initialisers at any time before the first static field access, not exactly at first use.

Example: with static int X = Compute(); and no static Foo() {}, Compute() may run earlier than you expect. Adding an empty static constructor removes the flag and makes it run precisely on first access, at a small cost in JIT optimisation.

code.title: Immutable Money struct with exact splitting

followUps:
Use a decimal and a currency table that records the number of minor-unit digits (JPY 0, USD 2, KWD 3), instead of assuming 2 everywhere.

Example: JPY 1000 has no fractions, KWD 1.234 has three, so a Currency value object holds Code and MinorUnits. Rounding and display use that number: Math.Round(amount, c.MinorUnits, MidpointRounding.ToEven). Storing integer minor units (1234 fils) needs the same table to convert back.

Outside the Money type, in a separate service or policy object that gets a rate for a date, because a rate is changing data, not part of a value.

Money stays immutable and only knows how to add same-currency amounts. A converter such as Money Convert(Money m, string to, DateOnly day) looks up the rate, applies it and rounds once. Keep the rate and date used on the stored transaction so that old totals can be reproduced exactly.

code.title: Emulating a with-expression: clone then assign

followUps:
You write a custom <Clone>$-style step yourself: with always makes a shallow copy, so to get a deep copy you copy the reference members inside the object initializer or in a custom method.

var p2 = p1 with {
    Tags = new List<string>(p1.Tags),
    Age = 40
};

Here Tags gets a new list, so changing p2's list no longer changes p1's. Immutable collections avoid the problem entirely.

Yes, since C# 10: with works on anonymous types and on any struct, besides records.

var a = new { Name = "Ann", Age = 30 };
var b = a with { Age = 40 };

The result is a new anonymous object with Age 40 and the same Name. It is handy for quick local shaping of query results, but anonymous types cannot leave a method, so prefer a record for anything shared.

code.title: Constructor enforces invariants, initializer cannot

followUps:
Putting [SetsRequiredMembers] on a constructor tells the compiler that this constructor already sets every required member, so callers need not repeat them in an initializer.

Example: required string Name forces new P { Name = "x" }, but a constructor [SetsRequiredMembers] P(string name) => Name = name; allows new P("x"). The compiler trusts you, so use it only if the constructor really assigns all of them.

Add a check after the initializer runs, because an initializer cannot see the other values while it assigns them: use a factory method, a constructor, or an explicit init accessor.

public int Start { get; init; }
public int End { get; init; }
public Range Validate() =>
    Start <= End ? this : throw new ArgumentException();

The factory Range.Create(1, 10) with a private constructor is cleaner, because an invalid object can never exist.

EF Core maps both as owned types (or complex types in EF 8+), which store their fields as columns in the owner's table and need no key of their own.

Example: an Order table gets Total_Amount, Total_Currency and Ship_Street, Ship_City. Configure with OwnsOne(o => o.Total) or ComplexProperty. Alternatively use a value converter to store Money as one string. Entities (Customer, Order) keep their own tables and keys.

In a domain service or in the aggregate root that owns the data, never in a single child object, because a rule across several entities needs a place that sees them all.

Example: "a customer's open orders may not exceed 5000" lives in Customer.PlaceOrder(order) if Customer is the root, or in an OrderPlacementService that loads both. Rules inside one entity stay in that entity's methods. Cross-aggregate rules may need a transaction or a later consistency check.
